newsitem.title: USA: U.S. health officials praise "mad cow" moves.
newsitem.headline: U.S. health officials praise "mad cow" moves.

text.p: Top government health officials on Wednesday applauded Food and Drug Administration moves to ban feeding processed animal parts to cattle to keep deadly mad cow disease out of the United States.

Officials told a packed congressional hearing that FDA action this month would remove a known health risk from the U.S. human and animal population. But they agreed continued vigilance and more research was needed to protect Americans from the dreaded disease.

Appearing before a House subcommittee on government reform and oversight were Michael Friedman, FDA deputy commissioner; Lawrence Schonberger of the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention; Linda Detwiller of the Agriculture Department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, and Clarence Gibbs of the National Institutes of Health.

Mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), is a fatal brain disease first diagnosed in Britain in 1986. More than 165,000 cattle from almost 33,000 herds have been diagnosed with the disease. Most of the stricken cattle have been in Britain, but cases have also been reported in other European countries. BSE has never been detected in cattle in the United States.

The possible link made last year between eating meat from cattle stricken with mad cow disease with a new strain of a fatal human brain disease -- Creutzfeldt Jakob disease (CJD) -- sent shockwaves throughout the world, and caused health regulators to review policies.

Creutzfeldt Jakob disease and BSE are both classified as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies. The leading theory for the cause of both is that they result from an accumulation in the brain of an abnormal form of protein known as the "prion protein."
Whether CJD can be transmitted through blood transfusions has been studied for years. Officials Wednesday agreed the risk currently appeared very small.
"This risk, is it exists, is extremely small and theoretical," said Schonberger.
"We have not been able to demonstrate any case of blood-borne CJD," said Friedman.
Lawmakers questioned the experts about the possibility of spreading CJD through cosmetics and dietary supplements that may contain animal products made from contaminated animals.
The health experts said these risks also appeared remote, but said they would study any new relevant data.
"We must be mindful of new information as it emerges," said Friedman.

The FDA will hold two public hearings next month on its proposed rule to ban so-called "ruminant to ruminant" feeding -- the feeding of processed animal products to ruminants such as cattle and sheep. The U.S. feed industry contends the ban would be unenforceable as proposed.
